newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asian Grain-Japan to buy beans, Taiwan to tender.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain-Japan to buy beans, Taiwan to tender.

text.p: Japan and Taiwan could provide the main action in the Far East grain and oilseeds market this week, while corn buyers in Tokyo and Seoul may be sidelined as they expect U.S. prices to slide further, traders said on Monday.

Japanese soybean crushers are expected to buy U.S. soybeans while Taiwan will hold tenders for 72,000 tonnes of corn, 12,000 tonnes of soybeans and between 64,000-96,000 tonnes of wheat, the traders said.
The Japanese buying may be prompted by an agreement that crushers recently reached with feed makers over local soymeal prices for October/December 1996 deliveries.

"Japan's soybean import business has accelerated since the start of October after the negotiations with local feed makers finished. We expect the high pace of purchases to continue this week," one soybean trader in Tokyo said.
"We believe weaker global soybean prices and Asia-Pacific freight rates have provided a good buying opportunity," he said.
Japanese importers have covered nearly 80 percent of their U.S. soybean needs for November shipment, and they have started buying U.S. soybean for December shipment.
Nearby freight rates on the U.S. Gulf/Japan route were quoted at about $19 a tonne, compared to $20 a tonne last week and $23 in June.
In Taiwan, the Flour Mills Association may place tenders for two or three 34,000-tonne shipments of U.S. wheat.

The FGEP group is expected to tender for a 54,000-tonne corn shipment and state-owned Taiwan Sugar Corp may tender for 18,000 tonnes of No.2 U.S. corn and 12,000 tonnes of No.2 U.S. soybeans, traders said.
But Korean and Japanese corn buyers will be absent from the market, dealers said.
"Most buyers appear to be taking a wait-and-see attitude as corn prices are expected to fall further," a trader with South Korea's Cheiljedang Corp said.
"Our target price for corn purchases is now moving to around $2.80 per bushel based on December futures on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT)," the trader added.
The December CBOT futures contract closed on Friday down 2-1/2 U.S. cents at $2.89-1/2 a bushel.
South Korean feed mill companies are seeking 5,000 tonnes of cottonseed meal on Tuesday for delivery by December 30 to the western port city of Inchon.

"Japan's corn premiums are easing. Well-covered Japanese importers don't have to rush to buy U.S. corn as they want to confirm the freight market's bottom," a corn trader at a major Tokyo trading house said.
Japanese importers had covered 70 to 80 percent of their January/March requirement for U.S. corn.
Premiums for U.S. corn are currently quoted at around 94 and 95 U.S. cents a bushel on the Chicago Board of Trade, against 98 and 99 cents a week ago, the traders said.
Japan premiums for U.S. corn for December shipment were quoted at 105/106 U.S. cents, little changed from last week.
In Manila, well-stocked Philippine flour companies remain fully stocked and have the luxury of waiting for further price falls before possibly entering the market.
